utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Do we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann, I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone, Mr. Khan and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the Defence appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my co-counsel, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Zeljko Olujic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Pavo Zdravko Mucic, together with my co-counsel, Michael Greaves, attorney from Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Your Honours, allow me, on behalf of my co-counsel and myself, to express our gratitude for not resorting to any disciplinary measures in relation to my client, but in order to clarify the whole situation, my client, after consultation with him, says that his intention was not to communicate with the witness who was appearing in the courtroom, but considering the position he was in, he wanted to give a sign to the translation service when the surnames Mucic, Masic and Music were referred to, which are three quite different surnames. So as to avoid any confusion he resorted to a means which is certainly disruptive and not acceptable in the courtroom, but he would like to express his gratitude to the Trial Chamber for showing understanding, but he wishes again to underline that he had no intention of communicating with the witness, but simply to allow each other to be able to see each other and to draw attention to the translation service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: My name is Salih Karabdic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic. With me is Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo, along with my co-counsel Ms. Cynthia McMurray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic, for your explanation of what happened yesterday. Nobody has any intention of antagonising either a witness or an accused person. All we want is for everyone involved in this case to understand the gravity of it. It is not a simple matter. It is complicated not only by social implications, but also the very freedom of those involved in it. All we are doing here -- and we expect them to understand that and appreciate that they should deal with everything concerning the trial with sufficient seriousness, to behave in a way, as you rightly said, he did not intend to disrupt, but definitely mere intention is not sufficient if the act itself can constitute a disruption. We appeal to everyone to appreciate that we want this trial to go on smoothly and without further incidents. Thank you very much. Can we have the witness now, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we have the witness brought in, may I make a remark, with your indulgence, your Honours. I should like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber that at the beginning of these proceedings it was stated, and the practice was for us to receive the transcript on the same day about 7.00 pm. However, this practice has been changed, so that for example for yesterday's proceedings, we have still not received the transcript. We were told that the rule was for us to receive it about 10.00 am the following day. This makes our work additionally difficult, because we are unable to check in time the transcript and to make any objections, if we have any. This change in the practice of the proceedings affects us in particular today, because in consultation with other colleagues we see that we have certain remarks to make regarding the interpretation of yesterday's testimony of the witness, and the transcript as a whole. The attorneys who speak both English and Bosnian have noticed many errors in the translation which change the meaning. I cannot be more specific straight away, and to point to this and that page or this and that line, because I do not have yesterday's transcript, but I should like to request that we review the tape of yesterday's proceedings and that the whole transcript be retranslated. This could correct some errors, because it is only possible to correct errors in translating the answers, but errors made in translating the questions cannot be corrected, and we should try in the course of the morning to repeat those questions that were incorrectly interpreted and to ask the witness to provide fresh answers to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the fact that this matter has been raised, on behalf of Mr. Delalic's Defence counsel, I should also like to ask the court to help us to follow the proceedings as well as possible and particularly to make sure that everything that is stated in the courtroom should be included in the transcript. Already during the testimony of Mr. Panzer, we noticed that important errors, and we drew attention to the head of the translation service immediately on the same day, that this witness was saying one thing and we have something else in the interpretation into Bosnian. This was not so significant when the questions were put to the witness by my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan in English and the answers were then retranslated into English, but those errors became much more pronounced yesterday when neither was the question put in English translated correctly into Bosnian, so the witness certainly did not understand that he was being asked; and similarly, the answer given on several occasions changed not only the names of people and places but also the very substance of what the witness was saying in answer to the question put to him. In addition, I must note that in this courtroom in the last few months, we have frequently heard the name Delalic used with, in addition, Zejnil, Zail, Emir, Sefik, Zajka and many other names, because I am sure the court already realises that we have large families with the same surname in that region, but we have been able to note that whenever the surname Delalic is mentioned, the first name Zejnil appears in the transcript. We have drawn attention to this and also listened to the tape and asked for the correction to be made, but to this day we have still not received the correction, and that is why we would like to ask the court, in addition to providing us with the opportunity to react in time to any such errors in the transcript, that also any correction that we make we must receive that correction on the relevant page at the latest within 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We should like to associate ourselves with what has been said by our colleagues regarding the question of translation, but we would like to note that specifically yesterday, the Music, Macic, Mucic and Fikret Masic were mentioned, whereas the transcript reflected Mucic, so this is a major cause of confusion which may not appear to be so significant for somebody who is not from the region and will not realise that we are talking about four quite different names. That is why I would like to fully support the previous colleagues in their statements. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am sorry we kept you waiting. It is a very serious complaint about misleading interpretations, thereby changing perhaps the nature of either the questions or the answers, so making it fairly difficult for one to determine what was being asked or what has been answered. That is a fairly difficult thing to resolve without inviting the witness again to repeat the whole process, because that is the only way we can correct that, except, of course, I do not know one can spot the mistaken words or names and then put that to the witness who then tells you what you understood by the names. The aspect of receiving the transcript the same day, I think that is the responsibility of the Registry and I think we will bring that to their notice so that they will comply immediately, so that will make it fairly easy for errors of this nature to be spotted immediately so at the next sitting we will know what to do to sort out mistakes. I suppose if the main problem is the interpretation, which is perhaps what I see, the whole picture, it means a more serious examination of who the interpreter is and how efficient that interpreter is, and I know there are quite a number of them. Since you have different levels of interpretation, it depends on -- but this is not a thing the Trial Chamber can itself handle. We can inform the Registry and they will take appropriate action. For the immediate problem, we perhaps will know what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honour, on behalf of the Prosecution I might say something by way of assistance to the Chamber. I think it is a very difficult job for the Chamber to try and deal with this particular problem, and I think it is brought about by the fact that the interpreters are given an enormously complex task in endeavouring to do the simultaneous translation, as your Honours may be more accustomed to the translation where the witness speaks and then the translator follows, which is another way of doing it. That probably tends to be slightly more accurate but is very much slower and would drag the proceedings down to a snail's pace. We do have the advantages of the simultaneous translation which may perhaps not always be as accurate, but in my experience of appearing in this court is extraordinarily accurate, having regard to the enormous task which these people are confronted with. Your Honours, I think there is a safety net and I think it exists and the safety net is that there is the simultaneous translation -- simultaneous transcript which is appearing on the screen that counsel are free to watch and if an error occurs to immediately draw that to the attention of the court and correct it. I am sure that your Honours would not be too disturbed if counsel did that because I think it is important if it can be corrected at the time. The other thing your Honours is that it is video recorded so the actual oral -- the voice of the witness and the physical image is still retained, so not all is lost. In addition to that, there is this process with the transcript when each day when counsel get the transcript they can go through it and correct it. I do not think it is true to say that whatever is recorded initially the first time when the witness speaks is the end of the matter by any means in terms of transcript. There is an opportunity to correct that. All these things are available and I am not sure it is a case of necessarily being one particular interpreter as opposed to another. I think there are going to be errors from time to time in this enormously complex process we are going through, where interpretation is not translation, it is merely a process of giving in another language what that is believed to have been said in another, and there is always variations, even in the most precise illustrations of it. Your Honours, in my submission, what I can suggest to counsel for the Defence is greater reliance should be put on the facilities that are available to them, such as the television, such as the transcript and such as the video recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My colleague wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, this colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: He is referring to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I am sorry, judge. I apologise. Sometimes I do not do real well in English. I do not do well at all in Serbo-Croatian, by sometimes my English is not very working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. Very briefly I would like to take the opportunity to beg, to remind everyone in this courtroom to speak slowly and clearly, because that helps a lot the work of the interpreters. It is really difficult from time to time to follow, especially some Anglo-Saxon speaking people. I am looking at you, Mr. Niemann. Please remind that, speak clearly and slowly. That really would help the work of the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to add a couple of things if I could for just a moment. In the first place, it is impossible for those of us who do not speak Serbo-Croatian, and I think that probably includes Mr. Niemann, to know whether the translation is accurate or not by sitting here and looking at our screens and watching it go by, so some of us are not in a position to do as Mr. Niemann suggests. The other difficulty, which I am sure is not absolutely clear to all the courtroom at this point, is that if the question is misinterpreted to the witness, then the answer may have little relation to what we thought we had asked the witness. Then I must also point out that during the testimony of Mr. Panzer, although I do not speak fluent German by any means, I speak enough German to know that on several occasions, Mr. Panzer's answer in German was, "Ich weiss es nicht", which means "I do not know", and it was frequently interpreted as "I do not remember". With regard to some questions that could be a profound difference. I did not feel comfortable enough with my German to rise and point that out at that point, but it was pointed out to me by some others outside this courtroom at a later time, confirming what I had thought at the time. I do want to point out the difficulty for those of us who do not speak Serbo-Croatian to try to correct this matter while it is ongoing. Perhaps as Mr. Niemann suggests and as Judge Odio Benito has just suggested, we do need to slow down rather profoundly when we are doing Serbo-Croatian interpretations because I understand the burden that is on those people up there in that booth to try to keep up with us and it is very difficult to do. Maybe the only solution is for us to be a little more vigilant, those who do speak Serbo-Croatian and for us all to slow down significantly so that the interpretations have the opportunity to be more accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with Mr. Ackerman. Let me expand on it for just a bit. In America one of the practices is if the lawyer is talking a little fast, the court reporter will just pipe up and say "slow down, I cannot get it". I am told by the court reporters here that is not the practice in the United Kingdom where they come from, but perchance, because both the interpreters and the court reporters frankly have a very difficult job, I cannot imagine how the interpreters can be listening to English coming out of my mouth and having Serbo-Croatian or French coming out of their mouths a few seconds later. They are thinking in two languages at once. I think they should be encouraged that if one of us, and I am sure I am one of the worst offenders, I will be the first one to admit it, is speaking a little fast or if the court reporters think we are speaking fast or speaking like we have a mouthful of something or other that they have to be encouraged to tell us to slow down, "Say it again", "I did not hear that", because going back and correcting the transcript -- I do not expect the judges to go through what, 6,000 pages of transcript now; I do not expect you to go through 7,000 to 10,000 pages of transcript trying to compare what you heard and what you have taken down in your notes to what the transcript says. That is asking more from judges than the law will allow. All three of the members of the Trial Chamber are going to rely to a great extent in reaching judgment, not just on the words on a cold piece of paper. If we are going to do that, we do not need judges sitting in this courtroom, we could just send the transcript back into chambers every day. It is the demeanour of the witnesses; those kinds of things go into your credibility judging function. Again just changing the transcript, although that may be great for the Appellate Chamber, does not help the Trial Chamber fulfil its function as a fact finder. Again I think that the thing that needs -- the interpreters and the court reporters and all of the staff and frankly the Trial Chamber -- if I am speaking a little fast and one of the judges does not understand what I am saying, for crying out loud, tell me to slow down, tell me to repeat it. That should go for all of us your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, the complaint we have received this morning mainly is one of accuracy in the translations -- what I would call interpretations, I would call it accuracy, and what appears on the screen. Now, often times here I have remembered counsel has pointed out to some inaccuracies on the screen and we have referred it to the translation booth and it has been corrected as we go. I suppose we can indulge in that a little more, instead of going through the whole thing and returning at a later date. Anybody who is able to pinpoint any errors of interpretation should be able to point it out at that stage so we do not lose sight of such things. I think we all have a responsibility for the accuracy of the record and I think we should take advantage of the opportunities that we have in achieving that accuracy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully endorse what you have said and I do indeed think that none of us have an easy task and that applies to the interpreters as well, and I would like to ask the court to caution me in the interest of accuracy to slow down, so that what I say is entered into the transcript accurately. But I would like to draw attention to one further problem that colleague Niemann has referred to, namely the transcript that we have in front of us, which can help us to react immediately to an error made, is not so perfect, because if a witness is speaking Bosnian Serbian or Croatian, my colleague sitting next to me who sees the English text, he does not know whether that is a correct translation or not, and myself, who speaks French, I am not able to note whether what has been said in Bosnian has been correctly interpreted into English, so the errors that we notice are mostly names and for instance the word sentence spoken by Mr. Panzer, the translation into Bosnian was sentence in the sense of a set of words rather than sentence in the sense of a verdict. I have also observed that the court reporters have a very difficult task, they have certain names that are already precoded and as I have said, as soon as the word Delalic is uttered, Zejnil appears, sometimes we do not notice it, but when we do and when we compare the transcript with the translation service, could we please have that correction within 48 hours, because otherwise we will have a backlog after 5,000 pages no one will be able to recall the objection we made regarding witness Antic and that correction has still not been made in the transcript to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I also refer to what my learned friend colleague Mr. Niemann has said regarding our ability to check the transcript. That is true, but it is also true what my colleague Ackerman has said with respect to the monitor. What happens in practice is the following: what is important is what the witness hears himself, he does not have a transcript, so if a name is incorrectly spoken to him through the interpreters he may give an incorrect answer, and how can we verify this? Only subsequently when we get the transcript. Therefore your Honours are quite right in saying that this process must be speeded up so that we receive the transcript as soon as possible to have the opportunity to react to it on time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is all we might be able to say here. You might perhaps as a backup to assist us also to put it in writing for the Registry, because that might make things clearer for everyone; not that they will not know what we have said here, but it will clearly indicate the urgency of it all. Can we have the witness? Invite the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is on his way I just want to thank you for your indulgence, listening to us pour our hearts out to you this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a very important aspect of the trial as a whole. Unless we get accurately what has been said on both sides, the decision will also not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the whole reason we are all here is to get --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The truth and justice of it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness is reminded that he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has not heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness is reminded that he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. WITNESS T (continued).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Good morning, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, while you were sitting out in the witness room in the last few minutes, I will be up front with you, I will tell you what was going on in the courtroom, we think there may have been some problems yesterday when I was talking to you in interpretation from my English to your Serbo-Croatian and then back again to English when you had answered, so I may ask you a couple of questions that are going to be similar to what I asked you yesterday and the only reason is just to clear up what some of my colleagues who speak Bosnian think may have been where you and I did not communicate. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, good. One of the things that was pointed out to me was that yesterday I asked you about food availability in Konjic amongst civilians, and I am told that your answer in Bosnian or Croatian was that there was a shortage of food and as I recall, the English translation was that food was fairly available. Which is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that there was food in sufficient quantities and that the population was not short of food like in some other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fair. I just wanted to make sure we were clear on that, sir. Going on to another subject, Grozdana Cecez. Regardless of what she said you did, set that aside for a second, what was your relation with her otherwise in the camp? Did you see her often, did you talk to her often, did you perhaps have coffee with her or share cigarettes with her, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relationship was quite good and our relationship was the same as with anyone else, especially an elderly woman, a woman whose age was the same as my mother's, I respected her. Very often I gave her a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So in March or April 1997, there would be no way that she could mistake someone else for you or you for someone else if she was using your name, would there?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I would object to that. This witness is unable to say what another witness does. I think he has brought out the facts but I think it is impossible for him to say. An improper question to ask: could she or could she not be mistaken about something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think so. It is a question he can answer. If somebody should not mistake you because of your relationship to them; you have met her frequently, you have known her, you meet often, she ought not to mistake you for someone. This is what he wants to find out. That is an opinion anybody can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was probably a mistake, because it was maybe one of the other guards who used my name when he was doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, she knew your true name when you were in camp, did she not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said maybe somebody else, another guard used my name to deceive, to cover up the trace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So she might have thought there were two guards in the camp with your name, is that what you are saying, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not say that there were two guards. I said one of the guards used my name to deceive her so that she did not know who did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So she would have thought there were two people with your name; someone would have made her think there were two people in the camp with your name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think so, it does not imply that. If somebody uses somebody's name, it does not mean there are two people of the same name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, I was suggesting that she might have -- he is suggesting she might have thought that there were two people with his name. Sir, let me go on to something else. In the early -- the beginning of the camp, when you were first assigned there as part of the HVO military police, back in May 1992, did not your duties include taking the list of names of prisoners being brought into the camp and taking down information about whether they had weapons or things like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Thank you very much, if you do not understand the question, for stopping me. I will rephrase it and we will work at it until you understand it. Back when the camp -- when you were initially assigned to Celebici in probably May 1992, that is the time I am looking at, did not your duties include things like writing down the names of the prisoners who were being brought to the camp and keeping track of who was in the camp, before you became the driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So your only duty was to take people to interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and later when the interrogation would be over, I was on duty by the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of caution I think we may have to go into private session for just a few seconds, for one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Sir, is it not true that with that woman Mira that she was in the camp for several days and that during that period of time you forced her to be a prostitute in the camp; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as I said yesterday on one occasion I drove her to the camp because her brother was imprisoned there and later I went to sleep and one of the guards took her to the place where her brother was imprisoned, I do not remember exactly which hangar or tunnel it was and what happened later to her, and the next morning at the gate there was screaming and I could see Hazim hitting her with the bat and trying to drive her away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So that is -- do you know a man named Skivo? You know him, do you not? He is the guy who had all the sheep on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man's name was Smail, not Skivo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was Smail Kovacevic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But his nickname was Skivo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his nickname was not Skivo. His nickname was Gurecin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How was it that you came to finally leave the barracks at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply left because since there were already some conflicts happening between the Muslim and the Croat forces and I did not feel safe any longer, and I just left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, that would not be that you were ordered out of the camp after the incident with Mira because the camp authorities thought that you were engaging in improper conduct; that would not be it, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, back in about August or September 1992 Mr. Delic did not come to you and demand your keys to the van and tell you to get off the post and never come back, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because he could not have ordered that because he was not the prison commander. That could have been ordered only by Zdravko Mucic whether I should leave or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you were not ordered off of the installation and told never to come back because of your activities involving Mira; that is what you are saying, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is not what you are saying or that is not true, which is it? You are not saying ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it was not true, I did not do anything with Mira and that was no reason for anybody to order me to leave the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. By the way, did you ever steal any binoculars that were property of the Bosnian army and sell them to the shepherd Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You do not remember whether you stole property of the army and sold it to someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is fine, sir, okay. Sir, early on when you were first assigned to the camp, what was the name of the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what his name was, but he was appointed by the forces of the Ministry of the Internal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Ministry of Internal Affairs, MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall an incident -- do you remember taking a man, one of the prisoners, into the room where you and the other guards slept? The man was an ex-policeman in Konjic and I understand your father had some problems with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father had never had problems with police in his life was he was a very quiet man. That is just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, is it true that you brought a man named Georgi Sipovac into the room where you and the other guards slept and gave that man some hand cream and had him put it on your legs and on your sexual organs and then perform a sex act? Is it not further true that while you were doing that you were laughing and when he was finished you had him sing a song, the words including "below the green mountain"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I am not a sick man to be able to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it not also true that after that incident you went out into a corridor with your automatic rifle, removed the firing pin so that it would not fire, then walked back into the barracks area, chambered a round, handed the weapon to this man and told him to commit suicide with it, and then watched while he pulled the trigger and heard the hammer fall and click?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It never happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to me. I do not know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever been convicted of a felony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You have never been convicted of a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified that after you took all of this property from these prisoners when you and the others passed the helmet and were forced to give it back, everything except some insignificant things were given back and I think you said some watches and gold rings. Do you recall saying that, sir? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Were those gold rings like the one on my hand? Can you see that sir? If not, I will take it off and have it shown to you. Wedding rings, are those the kind of rings you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said those were mainly old watches, things of very little value, things of no great value, no considerable amounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did I not recall you saying also that some gold rings were sold and not returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that some things were sold, but a very small amount. What was sold again was used to buy cigarettes and it was -- some of that was also given to the Serb prisoners as well and I believe that many of them would be able to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, if you would answer my question with the rings that were sold and not returned; did they look like my wedding ring?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought he had answered that. He did not think it looked like a wedding ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any possessions anywhere in the world that have what we would call a sentimental value, where the value to you is much more than the cash value of the item? If you like, I will give you an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those are personal items such as rings, watches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a second? (Pause). Sir, yesterday you were testifying about the hygiene for the people that were confined in the camp, the prisoners, and I remember you said they had improvised toilets; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thinking back to your own training in the JNA, would those be similar to latrines that soldiers would dig when they are out in the field, away from facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: When you were in the JNA you were stationed in a fairly large installation, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was a place that was designed to keep lots of -- where lots of people were to be stationed and to live and to work, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And because there were a lot of people that were going to live there, when the installation was designed it included a lot of facilities for cooking and for sleeping and for showers and toilet facilities and recreation facilities, and all those kinds of things that a large number of people need to live on, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The Celebici barracks were not designed to have hundreds of people live there, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, it was designed mainly as a place to keep supplies and store houses and warehouses and things like that, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was designed only to have a few soldiers live and work on the post, relatively few.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: About 30 or 40?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there were showers and kitchens and toilets and recreation facilities for those 30 or 40 people, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But there were not sufficient facilities for 200 or 300 or 400 people, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So the people that were in charge of the camp and the people that were working in the camp, you and all the other people in the camp had to improvise; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, for instance, there would be no way to have sufficient flush toilets for all of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Or showers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there were not beds available for everyone, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There just were not any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way -- your Honour at this point we will pass the witness and I will thank the court for its indulgence for letting me go over a little bit of what I went over yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday when the order was announced, it was announced that Ms. Residovic would go second and I would go last. With the court's permission, Ms. Residovic and I would like to change places so I go second and Ms. Residovic goes last. With the court's permission, that is the way we would like to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is your decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My name is John Ackerman and I will have a few questions that I would like to ask you. If you do not understand the question that I ask, could you please let me know that you do not fully understand it and ask me to rephrase it or repeat it in a way that you are certain you understand what it is I am asking you before you give me an answer. There was a time, was there not, in the earlier part of this year in the country where you are now living, that you gave at least two statements regarding experiences that you had at Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of those statements was to the Federal Police in that country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of those statements was made in the presence of a member of the Office of the Prosecutor from this Tribunal, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you make any other statements to anyone at any time prior to your arrival here in The Hague regarding your experiences in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made a statement on Monday and Tuesday -- on Sunday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That being here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But prior to your arrival here, did you make any statements beyond the two that I have brought to your attention this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. No, I did not make any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Since arriving here at The Hague, and now I want to specifically refer to the two statements that were made in the country where you now live, since arriving here at The Hague, have you had an opportunity to review those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So at no time while you have been here in The Hague have you seen and been shown the two statements you made to the Federal Police and the representative of the OTP in your home country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, the questions that I am going to ask you over the next several moments are questions that require your familiarity with these two statements, and so I think it is important, before I proceed further, that you do have an opportunity to look at them and to read them and to have some knowledge about what it was that you said on those two occasions, to have some significant knowledge about it, so then the question that I must ask you is; if they were given to you in the English language would you be able to read and understand them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the Office of the Prosecutor has translations of these two statements in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I then must request -- wait a minute, I think maybe we do have them here. Your Honour, I do have two translations in Serbo-Croatian. I know it is 20 minutes early, but I would ask the indulgence of the court at this point to rise and after I present these -- after I present these to the witness and for the witness to have an opportunity to go through them in detail before I continue my questioning, because it is very important in terms of the questioning I want to ask that he has reviewed the entire content of these two transcripts and be familiar with all of the things that he said in those two statements (redacetd) (redacted) I think it just makes more sense that he do this while we are not sitting in here waiting for him to complete it, that he have some time outside the presence of the Chamber to go through them in detail. That would be my request. Perhaps we could take the morning break now instead of 11.30 and accomplish it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it will be convenient. We will break now and assemble at 11.45. I had heard there was a mistaken mention of the home country. I did not hear it, but it is here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do not think I said it, your Honour. If I did, I certainly apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I did not hear that, but it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is exactly the complaint was, the translation that is coming on that is not what he said. I do not think he said the name of his present home country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might ask the assistance of the usher in presenting him with these statements before we rise, and Mr. T, understand that what we are asking you to do is during this break, very carefully read through these so that when you come back you will be familiar with everything that was said in these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can be allowed counsel to present his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any confusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly at some time the Prosecution will ask that they be marked, but Prosecution does not care if that be done before or after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree. They need to be marked at some point, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: When we reassemble, I think it will be the first thing to do to mark them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I missed the time you said we would reassemble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I need the Trial Chamber to understand that it is somewhat painful for me to raise another problem, because we have had plenty. Yet I am compelled to do so. It is my understanding that for some reason, the things that we all say to each other along this bench privately somehow make their way into the sound system and can at least be heard very clearly by the members of the audience. We do not notice in our own earphones, I do not know if the court can hear it in their earphones or if the Prosecution can hear it, but in the audience, I am told every time we have a private conversation here it comes over the earphones out in the audience, like the other day when Ms. Residovic and Mr. O'Sullivan asked leave to have a little conference here about some questioning, everyone out there heard their whole conversation. If they understood French, they knew everything they said. I understand just a moment ago when I had a little conversation with Ms McMurrey that it was heard clearly in the audience. I do not know what the solution to that is, whether it is to work on the sound system a bit, or for us to be very careful about what we say. I just need to bring that to the court's attention, because it is a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Keep your microphone off while you are talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently that is what we are going to have to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that might be the real problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I never hear what you say to your co-counsel. Maybe there is some special microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We need to examine the wiring system to see whether there is a communication between that side and those outside. We will look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe it can be solved and we will have to be very careful about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The two, a combination of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am ready to proceed, with your Honour's leave. Mr. T, during the break, you were asked to carefully review the two statements that we were talking about. Have you had an opportunity to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the witness, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During the break I asked you to carefully review the two statements you had made in your home country. My question now is: have you had an opportunity to carefully review both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is a matter which has to be -- I cannot proceed with questioning until the witness has had time to review very carefully these two statements. It is very important. I represent to you as an officer of this court that it is very important that that be done before I ask any further questions. I do not know how your Honour wants to solve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did he really understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me make certain that you understood my question. My question was: did you have sufficient time during this break to carefully review both of those statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I did not have enough time, and I do not really need to look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say you do not really need to look at it, are you telling me you are completely familiar with everything that is contained in those two statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not completely, I cannot recall having said some of the things that I read here, or maybe the translation is not a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I continue to take the position that it is very important to where I am going next that he have an opportunity to completely review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But he is not saying he could not take questions concerning those things. He is not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have told us, Mr. T, yesterday that you have -- I think you characterised it as a very poor memory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the time that you had during the break to look at those two statements, you have also told us that you noticed things there that you did not remember saying in those two statements, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said also that maybe the translation is not good. It is not the same as the tapes I listened to which I received in the country where I am living. I cannot exactly remember all that is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you last have an opportunity to listen to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was just once.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How long ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A month ago, almost immediately after the interview, maybe a month after the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, then, and preface it with this. Yesterday, in questioning by Ms. McHenry you indicated to this Trial Chamber that you had been untruthful in your statements in your home country with regard to whether or not there had been videotaping at Celebici. You told us yesterday that you had not told the truth about that matter, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wonder if, with the opportunity you have had now to look at these statements, you could tell us the other places in those statements where you were also untruthful, or do you need more time to review them to tell us the other places where you were also untruthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was untruthful with regard to one point only and that is the video cassettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So in the balance of the questioning that I have of you this morning, can I rely on those statements that you made in your home country as being truthful statements, other than the videotaping part of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You can say that without having an opportunity to completely review them; you are satisfied that everything else that you said during the taking of those statements was the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You told me a moment ago, before we broke, when I was asking about other statements you made, that you had made a statement here in The Hague on Sunday and Monday, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that a statement that was reduced to writing like the ones that are sitting in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not there was any kind of recording device used to record the statements you were making here on Sunday and Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, he corrected himself. Monday and Tuesday. Not Sunday and Monday, Monday and Tuesday. He corrected himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought it was the other way round, your Honour, that he had initially said Monday and Tuesday and then corrected it to Sunday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Sunday and Monday to Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, which days was it those statements were made? Was it Sunday and Monday or Monday and Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Sunday and Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question is: was there any kind of a recording device used while you made those statements, a tape recorder, a video recorder, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I saw, there were not any devices. Whether there were any hidden cameras or hidden recording devices, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution will represent there were no hidden recording devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Will the Prosecution also represent that there was no record of any kind made in the nature of a statement that should be furnished to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, I accept that. Mr. T, I want to ask you some questions about the time when you first arrived at the camp at Celebici, just to let you know what it is I am going to be asking you about, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us all here in this Trial Chamber that you believed that you were in the camp from approximately May through approximately November, that that was basically correct; is that what you told us yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be a period of roughly seven months, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other thing you told us yesterday was that you volunteered for the military, that you went into the military at the time the war started in the Konjic area; that is also a correct statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If it has been established in this case that the war started in the Konjic area in April, then it would have been in April that you first went in to the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly when the war started, but I did join at the very beginning of the war. What date it was, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If that was in April, then that would have been when you joined the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if it was April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP investigator in your home country, and I am referring to a BATES stamp page number of 4657, what you told the OTP investigator about that issue was that you had first reported to the military police of the Croatian Defence counsel and that you were there for three months, and after that you went to the army barracks in Celebici. That is what it reflects that you told the interviewer from the Office of the Prosecutor. Did you see that in the statement when you were reviewing it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that I made a small mistake, but I do not think that it is a significant mistake. First I went to the Territorial Defence and then I went to the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you now want to take the position, I take it, that what you told us here yesterday, that first you went to the Territorial Defence, is the truth of the matter, rather than what you told the OTP investigator a few months ago in your home country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I had made a mistake and I said that I went to HVO police first, but actually I was in the Territorial Defence first and I really see no reason why I should be lying about that. I just said without any reason to lie, I just forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Nor do I, and a moment ago you will recall that I asked you, other than the videotaping, was there anything contained in your statements that you were untruthful about and you told me there was nothing else contained in those statements that you were untruthful about.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. Forgetting something or making a mistake does not constitute being untruthful. I object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has already answered the question before your comment on its being truthful or not. He said he made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think so, your Honour. The rest of that statement, leaving aside the issue of whether you went into the TO first, that you served in the military for about three months before you went to Celebici, that part of your statement then would be true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly for how long I was there. I said roughly three months, was it three or two or one, I do not know. I really see no reason why I should be lying and why that is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The statement says: "At first I reported to military police of the Croatian Defence counsel and I was there for three months and after that, I went to the army barracks in Celebici." It does not say "approximately" or "roughly", it says "I was there for three months". Was that a correct statement you made to the Office of the Prosecutor investigator on that date or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, his answer was that he had said roughly and I am pointing out that he did not say roughly, that he was precise in that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not remember when the question was asked when I was interviewed in my country of residence, I could not remember within five seconds exactly when I was there, for how long was I in the Territorial Defence, when I went to HVO. I simply could not remember certain dates that happened five or six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You understand, do you not, that I am not asking you about seconds, I am asking you about months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The time I had to answer the question in my country of residence was a few seconds. I did not have too much time to think, to remember when I was there, when I left HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you talked to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, on March 24th 1997, you had given a statement about this matter to a representative of the Federal Police, had you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then after that statement, you were then asked to give an additional statement, and that was on April 28th 1997, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That statement went on for a significant period of time, over three hours, that you were being questioned by representatives of the office of the Prosecutor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Maybe it was three hours, but there were 100 questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you said at that time that you were in the military three months before going to Celebici camp, that was certainly your best recollection at that time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked about it even a second time during that interview, after you had had an opportunity to reflect on your answer, you were asked again about how much time you were a military police officer before you went to Celebici, and your answer was: "I could not say exactly, two or three months." So twice on that occasion you used the figure three months, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see no reason why this is so important exactly when I left, and for how long I stayed in an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please understand that I am not asking you to determine whether or not my questions are important. That would be up to the Trial Chamber. I am asking you questions that I deserve to have answered. You said it on two occasions at that time, did you not, that it was three months and then another time two or three months?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I just may correct the record, he said approximately two or three months and he estimated he started some time in February or March and said I cannot be sure. I would object to any further questioning on this line as both asked and answered and irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that Ms McHenry point out to me where in these statements he used the words "approximately two or three months". It is not in either place I have referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: On page 6, the question was: "I think you said three months? Answer: I could not say exactly, two or three months. Question: Well approximately. Answer: Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, that is correct, that is what it says. So the answer is approximately two or three months, is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I did say three months. I cannot remember exactly now, maybe I could make a mistake again in a month. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you went into the military in April and you were there three months before you went to Celebici, then it could have been as late as July before you actually took up your duties at Celebici. That could have been the case, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was before July, before July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If I may see if I can help you a bit more in trying to help you pin down this date and help refresh your memory about that; may I do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that same interview with the office of the Prosecutor, you were asked about medical care at Celebici; do you remember being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During our last break did you have an opportunity to review that portion of the statements you made to the OTP at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it, but I was not paying all that much attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to take you back again to one of my initial questions, and give you an opportunity to answer it differently if you would like to. That is: is there anything in these two statements that you noticed as you were going through them or that you heard when you were listening to the recordings that is untrue besides the issue with regard to videotaping, because if there is I need you to point that out to me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. It is true, is it not, that at the time of that interview with the OTP, you were asked if there were any medical staff available at Celebici. You answered that doctors would come from the city to check up on the prisoners. You were then asked: "So there was no medical staff actually in the prison, but medical staff from outside that would come and check? Answer: Yes." Those are true statements, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two Serb doctors who were imprisoned for a while, they were performing examinations of prisoners, but later, after they had been released, I went to pick them up, I cannot remember how many times a week, and I brought them there. They would spend the day in the camp and later I would take them back home. Mainly that was it for medical staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you told the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor was that there was no medical staff actually in the prison, but there were medical staff from outside that would come and check; that was what you said, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I forgot to say that they were there, they worked there while they had been imprisoned, that they were performing their medical duties. I simply forgot to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is that then another thing in your statements to the OTP that was not accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you not think it would be easier if you note those inaccuracies, put them to him, instead of asking him to remember what he read some time ago, which he has still not read properly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. If your statements to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor were correct and it was your position that there were no medical staff in Celebici and if it has been established in this case that the two Serb doctors you were talking about were released on July 22nd, then the three months that you have talked about of being in the military before you went to Celebici would put you there in July and after July 22nd when the two doctors had left, when they were coming from town and not resident there. That is a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this. First of all, this witness has already indicated that he was there before July and when counsel refers to him saying three months, he said approximately two or three months. He thought he started in February or more, which would have put him in the camp in May or June and in addition whether or not two Serb doctors imprisoned in the camp would constitute medical staff is certainly arguable and I object to any additional questions on this line of questioning as irrelevant, time consuming and asked and answered, and I would also note that I support the presiding judge's comments on the proper way to try to impeach this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms McHenry is now offering testimony to the Trial Chamber, which I think is interesting. I would prefer to get it from the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Put that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will, thank you. If what you are telling us today is correct, then I guess the position you are taking is that you were in the Celebici camp for a seven or eight months period from April or May, or somewhere in that neighbourhood, all the way through until October or November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that. Perhaps I arrived in April, maybe in March; I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We know, do we not, for certain, one thing we can be certain about is that you were working at Celebici camp on September 3rd 1982 because you have told us that you were at that party that we saw on the video here yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there on 3rd September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the 3rd September 1992, if I mis-spoke myself, we can be certain you were there on that date, correct, because of the videotape and your representation that you were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the date on the videotape is that, 3rd September, yes I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In addition you told the representatives of the Federal Police from your home country, in answer to a question, "how long did you perform duties at the camp?", your answer was "three or four months".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I made a mistake, due to my lack of memory. It was not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. During that statement, I think we have now discovered that in your statements to the Federal Police and in your statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, you made several mistakes due to your lack of memory; is that a fair statement of what you are telling us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You, of course, still suffer from that memory problem that you have described to us as you sit here and testify before this Tribunal today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, problem remembering dates and times, exactly when things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and so we must take the things you are telling us here with the understanding that you may be making several mistakes with regard to what you are telling us here, because of your lack of memory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, in cases of dates and times when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly will agree with me that there is a vast difference between telling us here that you were there seven months and telling the Federal Police that you were there three or four months. There is a difference between those, is there not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The objection is both asked and answered. He did not say he was there seven months. He said it could have been seven months, something like that, he is not sure of dates and times, so I object on both grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, your Honour, I am looking for something. I know it is here. (Pause). Your Honours, in yesterday's transcript, during the direct examination on page 7, lines 17 through 24, that is the LiveNote version of the transcript, the question by Ms McHenry was: "Just for an overview, how long in all did you remain working in Celebici? Answer: I remained about six or seven months, maybe a little longer." So that was the testimony from yesterday that I am talking about today. He said seven or eight months, maybe a little longer. You will agree, Mr. Witness, will you not, that there is a significant difference between seven or eight months and three or four months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If in fact you were only there for, let us say, three months, and we know that you were there on September 3rd, then you may have been there from September 3rd until December 3rd or from June 3rd until September 3rd or somewhere within three months of that date of September 3rd, if your statement of three months is accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was between the February or March until October, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back and ask you some more about these two statements that you gave in your home country. Both of those statements, of course, concerned the things that you observed and were aware of regarding your experiences in Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The things that the investigators who interviewed you were interested in were your experiences at the time you were in Celebici camp. Those were the things they were asking you about, that is what they were interested in, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They were interested in the things you knew about that went on in Celebici camp, the things you saw in Celebici camp, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The names of persons who were in charge at various times in Celebici camp, the names of guards who were stationed in Celebici camp, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You had an interview with the Federal Police that lasted about an hour, and then later an interview with the OTP investigator that lasted in excess of three hours, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that roughly four hours of relating your experiences at Celebici camp, you never once mentioned the name Landzo or Zenga during either of those interviews, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you take my word for it in reading through these statements that you never once in these statements mentioned the name Landzo or the name Zenga, or do you want me to give you an opportunity to read through all of them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then you did not give any more interviews regarding this matter until you came here to The Hague, when you were interviewed by Ms McHenry on Sunday and Monday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave no other interviews after the two in your own country until you came here to The Hague and you were interviewed by Ms McHenry on Sunday and Monday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So the next time you were asked about your experiences at Celebici after the two interviews in your home country was here in The Hague when you were interviewed by Ms McHenry; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were first interviewed by her on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was with her during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to my colleagues, but again the translation here, the colleague said, and it says in the transcript, as far as I can understand, that he had spoken in The Hague for the first time, but in the English text which we did not get as the translation, there are also words "when you were interviewed by Ms McHenry, is that right" so half the sentence was for us with no translation. Thank you. Excuse me, but this was without the translation for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are referring to the translation which is not an accurate reflection of the English version, yes? Is that what you are saying, that they are not the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly what I want to say. What was translated was up to "the next interview, you gave it in The Hague", that is what the witness heard as well as the rest of us who speak Bosnian. My colleague said another part of the sentence after the comma, which was "when Ms McHenry interviewed you". That part was not translated, nor did we hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that should be included in the Bosnian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will repeat the question so there is no question about whether the witness understood my question or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
