utterances.text: Yes, in the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, the question that I asked you which apparently was not completely translated; after the interviews in your home country, the next time you gave any statements about your experiences in Celebici were on Sunday, last Sunday, here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were interviewed by Ms McHenry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you got it right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think my next question then was: who was with Ms McHenry during that interview on Sunday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an interpreter and two other men whose names I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were the names of those two other men ever told to you during the course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I forgot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were they introduced to you as lawyers from this Tribunal, or as investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor, or how were they introduced to you? What was the role they claimed to be playing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As investigators working for this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was either one of them Mr. Milner who you had met with before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he only came during lunch. We did not talk about anything. He was not carrying out the investigation in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did either of those investigators ask you any questions or was it just Ms McHenry that was asking you questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main examination was done by Ms McHenry, only a question or two, insignificant questions, were put to me by the other two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On that Sunday meeting, how long did that meeting last? What is your best estimate of the length of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about -- from 10.00 in the morning until 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that meeting lasted for six or seven hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, there were several breaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then you met again on Monday with Ms McHenry, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were the same two investigators with her at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same two, plus another one who was a technician in charge of video recording, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was that the time then you reviewed some of the videos that we saw here in court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you again: did either one of the investigators during that meeting on Monday ask you any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple, but not very important questions. It was mostly Ms McHenry that was doing the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Some time during the questioning -- I want to ask you this: how long then was that meeting on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly the same as on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So another six or seven hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So prior to appearing in this Chamber to testify, you had spent somewhere between 12 and 14 hours with breaks in the middle of it, with Ms McHenry and these two or three investigators.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At some time during the Sunday or Monday when you were having these meetings, the name Landzo or Zenga must have come up during those meetings, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell me who it was that first mentioned that name during those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the first to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did Ms McHenry or any of the investigators that were present during those 12 to 14 hours of meetings use any particular kinds of techniques to help you with your memory problem, to help you remember things that you were having trouble remembering?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to any further line of questioning. I think Defence counsel has been given wide latitude. This entire line of questioning has been found irrelevant and in another Trial Chamber recently, in the Blaskic case -- I have not objected because I do not want it to seem like the Prosecution has anything to hide, but I am going to object to any further line of questioning, particularly when it talks about technique, I do not know what Defence counsel and I do not think the witness can be expected to know what is technique. I will represent we did not hypnotise him, if that is what Defence counsel is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She has correctly anticipated my next question, that is the next place I was going, because hypnotic enhanced memory is a major controversy in some jurisdictions around this world, and in most of those jurisdictions, the courts have taken the position that a witness may not testify if his memory has been hypnotically enhanced. That was where I was going, that was what I was trying to determine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually after he had answered your question, that he was not aided in remembering the names of Landzo, I do not think there was any need to adopt that line of questioning, because he did it unaided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept Ms McHenry's representation that no hypnotic enhancement was used and I think that would end that enquiry. Your Honour, I want to go into private session just for perhaps one or two questions just to clarify a matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back to an issue we have discussed a little bit this morning, Mr. T, and that is your statement to the OTP investigator in which you denied the videotaping at Celebici and your testimony yesterday that you were not truthful with the OTP investigator about that. That is what I want to talk to you about, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that you were untruthful about that because you were afraid, I think those were your words, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact your exact words were: "I guess because I was afraid of saying that I had taped it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it was or what it was that you are afraid of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was afraid to show the commander this tape. I thought he might shout at me for having filmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think perhaps you have misunderstood me. Maybe not. My question is this: you told this Chamber yesterday that you told the investigator a lie, basically, that you were untruthful with the investigator because you were afraid, afraid to tell the truth for some reason. Why were you afraid to tell the truth to the investigator of the OTP about videotaping, that is the question I want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason is that I was afraid to say that. I thought that they would scream at me, that -- I do not know. I simply did not say it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you are still misunderstanding the question. Why did you not tell the OTP investigator the truth? That is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. I was afraid because there were things on the tape where you could see that the prisoners were being mistreated, and I was afraid that if they were heard by the public, that I had made those tapes, that some of my relatives and family would have consequences, they would suffer as part of any kind of revenge. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be fair to suggest that you were afraid that admitting that would expose -- would perhaps expose you to some kind of accusations with regard to your role at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not afraid for myself, I was afraid, as I said, for my family, my parents, if one day this was leaked to the public, what was happening over there, down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it then that that same kind of fear would affect you with regard to other questions that might cause you to have some concern that they might be exposed to your family or to the public, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The factor motivating whether or not you were willing to be truthful with the OTP investigator was whether or not you were afraid that what you said might be exposed in some way and come to the attention of your family or other persons and bring discredit on them or upon you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Clearly, that same kind of motivation would make it necessary for you to also be untruthful about more serious issues like whether or not you had committed any rapes or murders, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that would not influence me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what you are telling us today is that you would be willing to be untruthful with the investigators about whether or not you did some videotaping at Celebici camp, but you would be willing to, if in fact you had been guilty of murders or rapes, you would have been perfectly willing to admit that to the investigators during that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I admitted the lie I told in connection with the camera. I admitted that, and if I had lied about anything else I would have admitted that too. As far as the video camera is concerned, I said that I had told a lie and I am now telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am going to go on to another subject. After a very short time in your duties at Celebici, your job was driver, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Once you became the driver, you had no other duties, that was your full time job at Celebici, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes I was on duty next to the telephone, as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So either you were on duty as a driver or at the telephone ready to become the driver if anyone needed you, basically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, while I was a driver I did those duties, and when I had no duties in terms of driving, then in the evening or during the day I would sit in the office where there was a telephone and answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "sit in the office", you are talking about the -- what we have called here the command building, the building where the offices were and some barracks and showers and things of that nature, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of regular working hours? Was there a time of the day when you started work and a time of the day when you finished work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. There were no precise working hours. When necessary I would have to do what I was told. There were no strict working hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you work seven days a week, six days a week, five days a week? Did you have days off that you could count on being days off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could sometimes take a day off, Saturdays or Sundays or some other day, but not very many, not very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that during that time that you spent a significant portion of each day you were working actually driving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not every day, sometimes it would be the whole day and sometimes no, but it depended on the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you were not called upon to drive at the time you were supposed to be driving, then I assume you were waiting for someone to let you know that you were then going to be called upon to drive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On your driving duties mostly what you were doing was driving prisoners who were released to their villages, mostly to Donje Selo because that is where most of them were going; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would happen as many as four or five times a week that you would be driving prisoners who had been released to their villages, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly how many times. I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to the office of the OTP in your home country, do you recall telling them that it was four or five times a week you would take them to where they lived; do you recall telling them that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the period of release sometimes more of them were released, sometimes less, so it depended. Sometimes I had to drive them four or five times, sometimes twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there were times when four or five times a week you would be driving prisoners to their homes who had been released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe not four or five, but not -- that does not mean literally four or five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you told the investigator from the office of the Tribunal that it was four or five times a week, you did not mean that literally when you said that, that was just something you made up figuratively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said literally, but not exactly. I could not know exactly. I could not recall exactly how often it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you told us yesterday, and I just want to make certain that I understood you correctly, that these releases of prisoners were primarily due to the efforts of Mr. Mucic, Mr. Pavo Mucic, who was constantly agitating for the old or the young or the innocent to be released from Celebici; that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic helped the Serbs as much as he could, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. T, you described for us yesterday, and I am changing now to another subject, you described for us yesterday an incident where --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may, may I just interrupt for one second, I am sorry counsel for interrupting. I just want the record to be clear. I just found the section where the witness was asked how long he drove prisoners home and I would just like the record to reflect in its entirety the full sentence the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no problem with Ms McMurray doing a re-exam if she wants to -- Ms McHenry doing a re-exam if she wants to correct something. I think it is inappropriate for her to interrupt my cross-examination for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Wait until you can correct this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay. Just let the record note that the representation of what was said was not accurate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can correct it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go to that part of the record that Ms McHenry is talking about, just to make sure we are all being fair here. If you will recall, you were asked the question: "How often would that be, do you think", talking about you taking prisoners home, "once a week, twice a week? Answer: In the beginning it was not that often but later on as the food was expensive and we could not hold prisoners, could not feed them, so it was four or five times a week that we would take them to wherever they lived, to their villages and he would be with me most often", he referring to Pavo Mucic. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To go on to the next subject that I wanted to raise with you, you described for us in your testimony yesterday an incident where a prisoner at Celebici by the name of Zara Mrkajic was "tied to a pillar, the electricity pile, the handcuffs, he was beaten before that and later he was tied to a pole and he was left there about four or five hours. They beat him while he was there." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You also told us that this was done by people from outside the prison, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that as far as I remembered, it was done by people from outside the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: After you had given that testimony, some time later, we all sat here in the courtroom and watched some videotapes, and one of those videotapes was of a party that was going on at Celebici where people were singing and drinking beer and that sort of thing. You remember viewing that party, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You identified one of the persons partying in that party as Zara Mrkajic, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That must be a different Zara Mrkajic than you were talking about being tied to the pole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is the same Zara Mrkajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence in the pictures that we saw yesterday that this person had been tied to a pole and severely beaten? Did you see wounds on his body, did he look like someone who had been tortured in those pictures that we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because those shots were made later, I do not remember how much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the videos were taken significantly after the incident you described about his being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know how much later, I could not say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Zara Mrkajic was a prisoner there at Celebici for quite a long time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was he there when you first went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not sure, but I think that he came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. But by the time of September 3rd in that party we were discussing yesterday, any evidence that he had been tied to a pole and beaten had apparently disappeared, because it was not visible, at least in those pictures; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, no traces of the beating could be seen. As far as I know, I did not see anyone else beating him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to talk to you now about your testimony yesterday with regard to the food that was provided to the prisoners at Celebici. You told us, I believe, yesterday, that the prisoners did not get enough food and the food was of poor quality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take it when you mean that the prisoners did not get enough food, what you mean is they were being slowly starved, they were not getting enough food to sustain their existence over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, they were given food once, twice, sometimes three times, it depended on the situation. The food was poor. Mostly they were not exactly starving, it was not really starvation, but they were not fed either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you say that they were getting enough food to maintain themselves at roughly the same weight and health that they were in when they came to Celebici, or were they all rapidly losing weight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that 90 per cent of them lost weight, 90 per cent of the prisoners lost weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I take you back again to the video that we saw yesterday when we saw the prisoner Zara Mrkajic, Mr. Mrkajic looked pretty well fed in that video of September 1992, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because before that he was rather a big man and he had certain privileges in the prison so that he did not go short of food.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So a man you have described as having been tied to a post and beaten severely had privileges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he acquired them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if this might not be an appropriate time for the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are still continuing with your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe so. I have another area here that I will probably cover.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may briefly make a request for your Honours' consideration. The Prosecution would request that all efforts be made to finish this witness's testimony today, so I do not know if your Honours would consider coming back 15 minutes or a half hour early for lunch and then if necessary going later this evening. I wanted to bring that to the court's attention, because there are some reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We might consider the end of the working day, there can be some extension.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, since my colleague suggested an adjournment, I took my headphones off and I did not understand the proposal of my distinguished colleague so if it is possible, I would like to ask her to repeat her request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What she has said is that cross-examination if possible be finished today and for that purpose we might cut down the luncheon break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: By 15 minutes. If then you heard my reaction, that was that we could continue, have a normal lunch break, come back and at the end of the working day, we might see how to extend and cover the rest of the cross-examination. Perhaps it depends on how the cross-examination goes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, but I thought you were continuing with the cross-examination, but you may bring up anything important.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise to you and to my colleague. However, the Registrar informed me that you have received our request; therefore to be allowed early next week to present our final argument regarding our request for removing all the evidence seized in Vienna, since today is the last day of the week I would like to ask you to decide on that. We have given our arguments in writing briefly and I think that I have repeated them on several occasions. We are given this right by the letter of the Prosecutor who, following the presentation of evidence with several witnesses from Vienna, informed us that Mr. Panzer would be the last witness that the Prosecutor would be inviting, therefore we would just like to ask the court to inform us and to reach such a decision that the final arguments may be offered early next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that will be convenient. We will take it early next week when we come back, I think on Tuesday, it is. On Tuesday we should be able to take it, about 11.00 on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I say something about the timing? Your Honours, it looks as though this witness will consume the rest of today. We have one witness -- there is two witnesses who have been here all this week and in fact one of them has been here since Thursday of last week waiting to give his testimony. He is going to be held over until Tuesday here in The Hague and we are anxious at least to have those two witnesses give their evidence as soon as possible, so that they need not be delayed any longer than is necessary. These issues -- these legal arguments, your Honours, are matters which in our submission are not so pressing as the concerns of witnesses who have been held here -- it will then be almost two weeks. In my submission, your Honours, after the conclusion of their evidence, if that is a convenient time for the Chamber, then by all means we can proceed with the matter then. I hasten to add that I do not anticipate that either of the two witnesses will testify as to anything that will touch upon the matters which could be concerned with this particular application. I do not foresee that at this stage, so it would be our submission that those two witnesses be permitted to testify so they can go home rather than having to wait pending what may be lengthy legal argument on these matters. Finally, your Honour, I might say that nothing I might write in a letter to the Defence gives anybody rights. That is a matter for the Chamber, not for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will consider it, which means you are likely to bring those witnesses on Tuesday the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tuesday and Wednesday, I would think. It will take two days for both of them to complete their evidence. They are here now ready to give evidence as the next two witnesses and have been here -- because the evidence has gone a little slower than we anticipated. Last time it went faster, so unfortunately it is not a precise business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You took the whole of yesterday examining this witness. The Defence is at least entitled to that much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not criticising anybody, your Honour. I am just saying the whole process is imprecise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr.s Residovic, are you agreeable to the arrangements so that after taking these other witnesses, we can now be free to take arguments at length, whichever way you want it. Are these other witnesses really related to anything concerning this argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, they are not. They are eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree for witnesses to be heard, but in any case, we insist that during next week, if the court can provide us with that possibility to offer our final arguments regarding our request, therefore this may be Wednesday or Thursday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that depends on the length of your cross-examination of these other witnesses, for you to consider Wednesday or Thursday. We should be able to guarantee that. You may now proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. T, yesterday when you testified in this court, you were asked the following question by Mr. Moran. It is at page 130, lines 18 through 20 of the LiveNote transcript: "You were at the camp essentially continually from, what, May 1992 through November 1992, October/November 1992? Answer: Yes, that is correct." Do you still abide by that or do you want to change that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May we have the microphone on for the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness's microphone should be on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it is on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I really cannot remember exactly a month or two, a month here or there, but something like that, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your position that you could have been there through the month of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was not there throughout November.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You think you left some time perhaps in the month of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. We do know for certain, do we not, that you were there on August 12th when the Red Cross made a visit to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if what you told the investigators in your home country, that you were there for three or four months, is true, and if in fact you were there until some time in November, then August through November would encompass that three or four month period, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is all right, thank you. I have one final matter. At the time you were being questioned by the OTP investigator in your home country, you were, of course, asked questions with regard to the allegation that you had committed a rape while you were at Celebici. You were questioned to some extent about that by the OTP investigator on the day that statement was made, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: One of the answers that you gave to that investigator regarding that matter was that: "And if I were to rape anyone, I would rape a 24 year old girl, not a woman of 60." You said that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is all the questions I have, your Honours. I would request that for the record, Ms McHenry identify for the record the two investigators, the names of whom this witness could not remember that were present during the 12 or 14 hours of interviews that went on here Sunday and Monday, for purposes of the rule regarding no contact between witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Certainly we are happy to answer. The persons present, depending on the exact time, were either Mr. Bart D'Hooge, Mr. Alistair McLeod with respect to the videos and Mr. Dan Sackson, who is a lawyer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that satisfy your enquiry?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is what I asked for and I appreciate it very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Let me just prepare myself a little. Good afternoon, Mr. T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I hope that due to this long examination you are not tired, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Regarding my conversation with you, I will hope to be as brief as possible so we can finish our work and return home happily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, during the previous day, actually the day before yesterday, I asked to establish contact with you and to speak with you. Have you been informed about that, that I as Defence counsel, to introduce myself, my name is Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Zagreb, defending Zdravko Mucic, I said that I would like to have personal contact with you, have you been informed about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: May I hear the reason we have not met and why we have not spoken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a headache and I was tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was that what you wanted or somebody suggested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. T, during the examination-in-chief when you were interviewed by the Prosecution representatives that following your arrival to Celebici, the camp commander was somebody from the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you, Mr. T, know what the gentleman's name was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something else that I forgot to mention at the very beginning, and that is that during our conversation we both speak in the Croatian language, but all this is being translated to the official languages of the court, i.e. English and French. Therefore, I would like to ask you, when I am asking the question I would like to ask you to wait for the answer. You will hear the translation and then you should wait for the end of the translation, once you hear that you can give your answer to me and please try to be as slow as possible in your answers so that the interpreters can give us a precise interpretation. During your examination-in-chief, on one occasion you said that when Mr. Mucic was the commander, that he spent an hour or two in the camp and literally, I quote: "He was away rather than there." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, please tell us, did Mr. Mucic ever stay in the camp overnight, as far as you know, or he slept outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that he stayed overnight once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Only once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also during the examination-in-chief, you said that there were no instructions for the guards in the camp, there were no meetings held, nor anything like that regarding the organisation of the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, you also mentioned a Mr. Bato Kuljanin and you said that he was physically mistreated, but by people from outside the camp, and you said precisely that those people were members of the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Bato Kuljanin was not mistreated by the camp guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, tell us if those gentlemen from the MUP were armed. Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably yes, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mucic have disarmed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if he was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But when that was the situation, was Mr. Mucic able to disarm, so to speak, the men from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, same as I was not able to prevent them from coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And why was he not able to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because those were people who had been on frontlines, those were the ones who had captured the prisoners, so they used to come down to take their revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How did those people come to the camp to start with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Which gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: The main entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, in view of everything that my predecessors have asked you, I do understand that it has been quite a while and you cannot remember everything, it has been five years and people wish to forget things, but can we state that you actually cannot precisely remember, cannot precisely decide on certain times and dates regarding things that had happened during the war that happened in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have problems remembering the exact times of certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, have you ever committed a criminal offence, a criminal offence as defined by the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the country where you are now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was charged with a murder in Bosnia-Herzegovina that I had not committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How were you charged and tried? Were you present or was it an in absentia trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That trial was by force, under coercion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you hold any rank? During both examination-in-chief and cross-examination, you told us that you had been interrogated in the country of your present residence by the federal officers and second by the representatives of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: My question is: if you had known that you could be on trial or you could be charged with rape, that there were such charges against you, would you have requested presence of Defence counsel on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically, if you had known that you were being charged with rape, that somebody -- if somebody had informed you about that, would you have requested immediate presence of Defence counsel, so if there is justified suspicion against someone, would you have requested presence of Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think it is improper and unfair to ask this witness to answer hypothetical questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can put your question to him. Ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you were interrogated by representatives of your present country of residence, you were told that there are charges brought against you for rape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not told that, I was just told that somebody had accused me of rape.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But why did you not ask for your Defence counsel to be present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not do it, therefore there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you feel totally innocent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, since 1992, when you left the area of Konjic, has any organisation or anyone else ever told you what you should say or what you should testify to if you are invited to the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What do you think, why, when you were interrogated, why did the investigator tell you at the very end when he asked you about what you had known about Mr. Mucic and he said that certain people were blaming you for rape, why did he not tell you so at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Where is your wife? You do not have to tell me directly. Is she living with you? Is your wife living with you in the country where you are coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you married when you were in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said that you had been a driver. You did serve your duty in the JNA. When you were with JNA, were you a driver as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you asked the investigator, the representative of OTP to give you an answer regarding your loss of income during your stay here, were you satisfied with the answer you received regarding the compensation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but now I am being told that not everything can be compensated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said during examination-in-chief that you knew Mr. Mucic. Has Mr. Mucic ever proposed to you anything that could be illegal such as black marketeering, soliciting, blackmail, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic hold any military rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic ever order you to do anything that could be considered illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has Mr. Mucic ever told you that he had seen a person being raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has Mr. Mucic ever told you that he knew or had known about any beatings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Just what you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never told me he had seen any beatings, but since -- he used to receive reports from Hazim, I do not know if he had told him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I am asking about your experiences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has he ever told you about knowing about killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Has he ever told you that he had seen torture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mucic ever harsh with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, before the war had you ever seen a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In films.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But not in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were you able to tell the difference between JNA camouflage uniforms, those of the Territorial Defence, HVO and others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were all more or less the same uniforms with some different insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that members of the MUP had come inside the prison. Was reserve police force ever going through the prison as well, the reservists? Did you see them there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I did not understand, who are reservists?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With regular police, there was also the reserve police force, the reserve police forces, those who were not regular policemen with salaries, but those who worked as reserve policemen, exactly that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you see other uniforms in the camp, in the prison? You described the MUP. Did you see people wearing other uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were members of Mitke Pirkic, then sometimes Rale's soldiers would come and maybe some others, but I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you feel when you heard that the investigator, when you were being interviewed in your home country, and when you were told that Mr.s Grozdana Cecez claimed that you raped her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you feel blackmailed as a result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. What do you mean blackmailed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said you felt awful. Could you explain that a little? Were you empty, were you emotionally distressed as a result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was very upset, I could never imagine that anyone could tell such a lie about me, especially someone I had helped. So I was literally flabbergasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, please tell us how you felt at the beginning of the interview, when the investigator said that he would question you on the basis of the requests from the Yugoslav Tribunal for war crimes in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you clarify that please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: From the translation that you received today and read, you saw that the interrogator said that he would be questioning you on the basis of a request from the Yugoslav Tribunal for war crimes in The Hague. How did you feel then? Did you feel afraid that some one from Yugoslavia wanted to question you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived at the Celebici prison there were some civilians there, but that the majority were those captured around Bradina and Donje Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said that they were prisoners from Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And were there people from Bradina too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was any fighting there, or did the Croatian and Muslim forces enter those places without any resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, some places there was. In Donje Selo there was not much resistance, but in Bradina and Brdjani there was some fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Who put the resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb population, the Serb inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were they organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did they have their commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly whether they had commanders. There were some locals there, they may have been in charge. Yes, I just remembered, there was Vlado Cecez, he was in Donje Selo and I think Mica, I cannot remember his surname, he was from Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. T, let us go back a little to the situation in the prison itself, while you were there, of course, because I am asking you only what you know from personal knowledge. Did the prisoners have a morning salute with the playing of a hymn and saluting the flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prisoners? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did any such event occur for the soldiers or the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very rarely were there any such events, but without a flag .

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you exclude the possibility of this having been a regular affair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What was the discipline like in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite good while Pavo was there. When he left, then it was quite a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts among the guards when Mr. Mucic was not there, amongst themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, perhaps yes, perhaps no, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you something, of course if you can remember, whether somewhere in the autumn you ever crossed into Serb held territory together with Mr. Zdravko Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we took the prisoners to Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that was the competence of the Serb forces, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But can you remember ever crossing into Serb held territory with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, we went to a -- what is its name, somewhere near Kresevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Fine. How did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was this under Serb authority? How did they receive you when you got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see anyone. I stayed at the checkpoint, I could not go any further. I do not know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. T, thank you, your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I know that you are rather tired. I shall try to make my questions brief and clear and I ask you if you do not understand any question to tell me immediately so that I can repeat myself and make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my questions also briefly and precisely, of course if that is possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the warning made a moment ago by my colleague Olujic, please bear that in mind, because the two of us speak a language we understand very well, and you can answer my question very quickly. However, what is most important is that everything we are saying should be understood by the Trial Chamber and the other colleagues in the courtroom, so that please when I put a question to you wait for the interpretation in the headphones and answer my question then, so that there will be no problems with the interpretation of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, you were born and grew up in Konjic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, you were in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in Konjic when the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina occurred at the beginning of April 1992, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, you were aware that all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and particularly members of the Croatian nation were following closely what had been happening the previous year in Croatia, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware that in Konjic the Croatian people started to prepare for the possible untoward events that actually occurred later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that everyone was preparing, both the Croatian and the Muslim people started to arm. I do not think that some people started early and some later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said in your testimony, Mr. T, that you as a soldier were assigned to the Celebici prison by your commander, Zeljko Brekalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Brekalo was a commander of the military police of the Croatian Defence council, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. T, do you know what position in the HVO military police Ivo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, we did not get the surname. Could counsel please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what position in the HVO military police was held by Ivo Vujicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he was the main boss for the Croatian police, for the operations in Donje Selo. I do not know what rank he had. I think he did not have any rank. What happened with him later I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at that time, the time we are talking about, that is April/May, the period you are testifying about, Ivo Vujicevic was commander of the HVO military police of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not the commander, he was some kind of a special fighter. He volunteered, he came from abroad. He was head of the operations in Donje Selo on behalf of the Croatian police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. T, you also said yesterday that there was a short interruption in your stay in the Celebici prison, and among other things you said the reason was that at that time, what you described as the Muslim police, had been formed. My question is: are you implying that at that time the military police of the Territorial Defence of Konjic was being formed, is that its official name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of the aggression, Mr. T, is it true to say that in the HVO military police to which you belonged as well, there were quite a number of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The formation of the military police of the Territorial Defence occurred much later, somewhere around the beginning of July; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly when it was formed, but it was later, after the formation of the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And only then a part of the Muslims from the HVO military police switched over to the military police of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said, Mr. T, that certain clashes occurred between the commands of the HVO and the TO, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall that somewhere at the end of June and throughout July there were battles near Borci and Glavaticevo in which the Croatian Defence counsel forces did not participate; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that that was the initial cause of the mentioned conflicts between the HVO and the TO in Konjic at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. This is the first time I am hearing of that reason. I have not heard it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that when yesterday you were saying that members of the HVO police had withdrawn from the Celebici prison, this occurred at the time when the military police of the TO was being formed and when you yourself were absent for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a citizen of Konjic, you joined the war at a very early age, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the reason, Mr. T, why yesterday in answer to one of the questions put to you, you responded spontaneously "gentlemen, there was a war, you understand it was a war". Do you remember this response on your part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you can remember that for you as a young man, war and the horrors that started to happen in Konjic were a terrible experience, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm in this court that the shelling of Konjic started on 4th May and that after that there were dozens and hundreds of shells falling on Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please let the witness answer your last question. Kindly repeat it so he can answer, because he did not answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, can you confirm that from May 4th heavy shelling of Konjic continued on a daily basis and that there were dozens and hundreds of shells dropping on the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, they were coming from planes and from Serb held territory in Borci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those shells hit people in the street, people in their apartments, schools, hospitals, the hospital, industrial and other facilities, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we were cautioned a moment ago, my question is much longer than your answer, so before you answer it please wait for the interpretation into English so there will be no confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am listening to the Croatian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but on these other earphones on the table you can hear the English interpretation and when that is over please answer the question. Thank you. Can you tell me, Mr. T, whether it is true that Celebici is about 10 kilometres south of Konjic in the direction of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that, 10 or 15 kilometres -- 10, yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is an area that was not subject to daily shelling, as was the case with the centre of the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, maybe some shells fell on Celebici only two or three times in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore from the standpoint of shelling, the Celebici area was safer than the area of the city centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was safer, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, can you tell me whether it is true that after the liberation of Bradina, several thousand refugees came from Eastern Herzegovina and Eastern Bosnia who had previously found shelter on the slopes of Bjelasnica and Treskovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know which refugees you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslim and the Croat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I am not aware of that. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were quite a number of people from Eastern Bosnia, from Zepca, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the town at the time there were several thousand new refugees, were there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All this caused a great deal of difficulty in terms of accommodation and food for these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the former JNA, you had served in the artillery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These shellings of Konjic after May 4th were artillery shellings using heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they came from the eastern side, from Borci, that is from positions held only by Serb forces; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The town was shelled from those positions until June 1993, when you left Konjic; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, you said in this courtroom that there was a commission in Celebici which interrogated the people detained in Celebici. Are you aware that the first President and head of the investigating commission was the former judge Goran Lokas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to remind you -- let me first ask you whether you know Goran Lokas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you; do you know Ljerko Kostic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name sounds familiar, but I cannot remember his face.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to remind you and ask you whether it is true that he later on became head of the investigators who were questioning the prisoners, would you recall him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot, I am sorry. I remember somebody called Kuhar and another one who was also quite an elderly man, he was also working in the Ministry of the Interior, but I cannot remember them exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware, Mr. T, that the commission for investigating prisoners also determined the categories to which those prisoners belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you also know that at the very beginning the commission released about 50 detainees who did not have any weapons nor were in any way linked with the blockages in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember there were two minor children who had been released and there were elderly people released, but number I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that that was done by the commission which was questioning those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. T, you said yesterday, and I will quote from the transcript, about the stories in town and the things you heard from the guards regarding Zejnil Delalic. You heard that he had been in charge of Prozor and Konjic; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also hear from Mr. Mucic that Zejnil Delalic was later the commander of the Tactical Group 1, also from these other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from other people, I do not know if I heard from Zdravko Mucic. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you probably heard from Zdravko Mucic that he knew Zejnil Delalic quite well because before the war they had both worked in Austria; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the occasion when you spoke with Mr. Mucic, Mucic was actually telling you about how he could address Mr. Delalic freely, that he was closer to him than to others and that he believed that Mr. Zejnil Delalic was willing to help him if he was able to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also in conversations with Mr. Mucic hear that he was for certain things free to address Mr. Delalic and that he was certain that if Mr. Delalic was able to do something to help, that he was certainly going to do that; is that the way Mr. Mucic told you about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, in this courtroom, you said that you saw Mr. Delalic in Celebici twice, once at a party and once when he was in Mr. Mucic's office. Please tell me, were you present in the office where Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were never present in their alleged conversations and meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said that you saw Mr. Delalic for the second time at a party, so I am asking you now: was that a party in the second half of August where a solemn oath was declared by members of the Territorial Defence? Is that the celebration we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time the soldiers of the Territorial Defence of Konjic, they were giving their solemn declaration before their commander Salem Ramic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during this celebration, Mr. Delalic came from Igman and greeted the soldiers who were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if he had arrived from Igman. I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But that is the second time when you saw Mr. Delalic, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, in the statement you gave to the investigator in your country of residence, you said that the Celebici barracks was a huge facility where up to 10,000 soldiers could be accommodated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said that up to 10,000 people could be accommodated there, detainees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom, you said that as far as you could recollect, in the Celebici prison there was a total of 120 to 150 prisoners and that they were accommodated only in three buildings; did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if it is true when I say that the space where these prisoners were was smaller than -- was less than 5 per cent of the entire territory of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you, is it less than 5 per cent, the small space that you talked about, is it less than 5 per cent compared to the space where you said 10,000 people could be accommodated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. T, you also told the investigator that in this huge barracks, there were many other facilities, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. What facilities?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Warehouses for the Territorial Defence, the tactical group, there were soldiers accommodated, weapons were repaired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this courtroom you also said that there were many people coming and going to and from the barracks for different reasons, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, I would just like to go back a little to the statements you had given earlier to the police from the country of your residence and later to the investigator from the OTP. Is it correct, Mr. T, that the representative of the Federal Prosecution informed you that the interview with you was being conducted on behalf of this International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. T, when he informed you that there were certain accusations against you for the murder of Zeljko Milosevic, that at the time, at the same time, he said, and I quote: "Evidence the Tribunal has at the moment indicates that that is not true."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after that, you were still willing to speak about certain things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the same as before, same as I had spoken earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to check some things with you, namely: before the investigators of the Tribunal at the time, you said that you had first registered with the military police of the Croatian Defence Council, that you had spent three months there and in this courtroom you said you were first with the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I had made a mistake. I was first with the TO and later I went to the HVO police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. T, that immediately after that reply, when asked by the investigator when you applied to the military police, was that a form of mobilisation, or was that your choice to go there and register with the military police, you said "that was my choice"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you answered that at the time the military police was known by the name HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you also presented reasons why you registered with the military police, and reasons which you repeated in this courtroom as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time you said that you needed to know people to have connections in order to facilitate your registration with the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you quoted your unfortunately deceased friend, Mladen Pehar, as the person who helped you with registration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you said that you were at the time officially issued an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that you had a piece of cloth which indicated HVO on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when I went to HVO police I got the insignia. Until then I had been with the TO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time, same as today, you said that you were sent to Celebici by your HVO police commander Zeljko Brekalo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, were you wrong about all these things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. T, you went to Celebici as a member of the HVO military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So at the beginning of the war, you were not a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said first I was TO, then I went to the HVO police, because at the time HVO police was providing guards to Celebici, so I was a member of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. T, I do not want to confuse you with months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you did not confuse me, I gave an excellent answer -- a truthful answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mobilisation to Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I moved to HVO police and then I was transferred to Celebici to the prison as a member of HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The war in Bosnia started on April 6th. That is when Bosnia was declared independent, and on 9th April Bosnia-Herzegovina declared mobilisation. I believe the transcript contains all your statements and your answers. I think we will be able to see whether you were saying the truth or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you passing the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I thanked and I am finished with my cross-examination. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not have any re-examination. I would ask that the statements of the witness to the Office of the Prosecutor representative and to the Federal Police be admitted for the purpose of showing the extent to which this witness has and has not been impeached, not for the truth of it -- for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I can understand has been impeached, but I do not understand has not been impeached.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: For instance, your Honour, it is the case that at various points, even though the witness might have said three or four months, when asked when he left the camp, he would at other points have said, "I do not know exactly, it was somewhere between September, October, November", and those kinds of things -- for instance, there was another: Defence counsel for Mr. Landzo indicated that he had never talked about Mr. Landzo before. When you look at the statement you see he was never asked to give the names of any guards or the names of anyone he saw mistreating anyone.
