I think those are relevant to the cross-examination and so we are not asking them for the truth, but to the extent Defence -- every single Defence counsel has used that statement to attempt to impeach him, I believe it is proper and I believe this court has previously found in such circumstances, it is entirely proper for either party to ask that the statement be introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When you say has not been impeached, you mean you want to corroborate his statement to the court, that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not know corroborate, but one with respect to Mr. Ackerman's question, I believe the Prosecution is entitled to show what he was and was not asked, and with respect to other Defence counsel, who took out certain parts of what he said. When you look at other parts they clarify or amplify what was asked of him, so I think it is directly relevant to the extent to which he has been impeached. Again, I would not say it is for corroboration, but it is for to the extent that on various issues, the Defence counsel has attempted to impeach him, and has in fact -- the witness has often correctly stated, "Well I did say X". In another point, he may have clarified it, and I think it is important, and only fair, for your Honours to have both portions in front of you. We are not trying to seek it for the truth of anything that has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you appreciate that at the time the statement was introduced, it was your obligation to have asked why it was introduced at all and if it was for the purpose of impeachment then they should have brought it in. That is what should have happened, but now if all you are doing is suggesting that it should now be tendered in evidence then you should say why it should be so tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe even Defence counsel will concede that they showed him and referred in detail to his statement for purposes of impeachment, because I believed that -- I was not aware that I specifically had to ask for what purpose they were doing it, but since I believe that even Defence counsel would have to concede that it was for purposes of impeachment, rather than interrupt the flow of their cross-examination, as we have in past occasions, I thought it most efficient and most courteous to wait until the end and just ask that the statement be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the statement being tendered at this stage? It has all been effectively and efficiently used in cross-examining him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I first have an objection to the continued practice of Ms McHenry to testify as to the contents of documents and things of that nature. In the process of offering this she has now represented what much of the contents of it are to this court. I think it is improper. She repeatedly is suggesting in the course of speaking objections, the witness hears what she would hope his response would be to the question that has been asked and now she has told you what she thinks the statement contains, that you should be interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. If you remember, when you were proceeding with your cross-examination, asking him to deny certain things in the statement he made, I asked you to put those things to him, which you think he now would deny or admit. It was at that stage I thought perhaps that foundation for impeaching him might be laid, and then the prosecution would have a purpose for witness statements being used, but since everything has transpired, it showed that that statement was a background for your cross-examination, it is deserving that it should be tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We should have that statement to which you have been referring for the purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next thing I wanted to say was, on behalf of Mr. Landzo, i have not objection to you seeing the statement, because you will find when you look at it that he was indeed asked about the names of guards, and said he could not remember, he was sorry, it was too long ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: From the transcript we have these things will now be obvious, whether this statement is what he remembers or does not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have no objection to it, except to the extent that to admit it to show the purpose for which he was not impeached? If I choose not to ask him about some inconsistent statement, does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is a fairly difficult way of putting the reason why it is being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think it is perfectly fair under the rules of this Tribunal for the Tribunal to have the statement in front of them -- not for the truth of the statements in there, just to show how -- just to judge his veracity, and for that limited purpose we would have no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the only reason for which it could even be --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour, but terms of Ms McHenry's tender made it seem a little wider than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think she thought of anything else. Yes, do you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wish to support my colleagues that the motion to adopt is in a very limited form. We have already discussed this one. Statements do contain facts that have been included neither in the examination-in-chief nor was there any discussion in this courtroom. Therefore, we do not speak of those statements as evidence proving the truth of the facts. I asked for a redaction and I know the court did not accept, but if these situations are to be repeated in the future, perhaps we could consider that a part of those statements are adjusted to the purpose for which they are tendered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We have nothing new, we join in what our colleagues have said previously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will admit the statements tendered to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are not substantive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. The Prosecution is not offering them as substantive evidence, only that they relate to the credibility of this witness with respect to what he has stated on this stand. I believe the Registrar already has the Serbo-Croatian versions and here are the English versions which I will offer. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Without the statements in, his evidence might be lopsided. It would not be complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I just may also briefly respond, the Prosecution, me in particular, does not want to give evidence but when I am asked a question, sometimes I believe it to be appropriate to give a proffer, particularly when asked about it. I do not wish to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We understand your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What was being contested was referring to the content of the document itself in answer to whatever question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is the case that sometimes your Honours ask a question and in making a proffer of the relevance or the reason, it is entirely appropriate and proper for counsel to give the -- for the Prosecution attorney or the Defence attorney in fact, as Mr. Ackerman just did, to give a proffer of why it would be relevant and appropriate for the court to have this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just before the break, just to offer an aside, if I may. It is always said in the English courts that evidence comes from the witness box, not from counsel. I suspect that is the case in every jurisdiction which we represent in this court. That is the first thing. The second thing is this: my learned friend Ms McHenry has advanced her own courtesy. Can I just say this by way of compliment I hope to her, that she is always unfailingly courteous and that is something we appreciate. I may disagree violently with what she says, but she always says it courteously. That should be a lesson to us all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that is the end of this witness's testimony. He is discharged. That is all we have to do for the time being. Is there anything more for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have another witness. I am not sure whether he is on his way or already here, but anyway we have another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All right, we will take him at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, I think you are in charge now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We call Mr. Rajko Draganic as our next witness

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please swear the witness. Let him swear. RAJKO DRAGANIC (sworn).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rajko Draganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 28th September 1952 in Brdjani, Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your ethnic group, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, what education did you receive? I mean, what kind of schools did you attend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed secondary school for the drafts. I am a woodworker and I operated construction machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say exactly what was your profession at the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in Libya, in construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a time when you went back to Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Brdjani on 28th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, was Brdjani a village with Serbian majority? Can you say what was the ethnic composition of Brdjani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 70 per cent Serbs and 30 per cent Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you find to be the relationship between Serbs and Muslims in the village of Brdjani when you arrived there at the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could already feel that war was in the offing. Some had good relations, some did not. We were each afraid of the other and then the worst happened that should not have happened, but up to the war, relations were good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there any negotiations between Serbs and Muslims in your village at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 10th May, I was at home. We had agreed to meet at the house of Mehmed Bukvic. We made a minutes of the meeting that we would not touch each other, that everything would be fine, but when I got home the shooting started and that was when we retreated to Bradina and that was when war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you do with the minutes of this negotiation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not know what happened to the minutes. I did not sign it, so I could not tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened then? What happened after May 10th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, with our women and children, went to Bradina, because Bradina was predominantly Serb populated, so we thought we would be safer and then on the 25th, Bradina was attacked. It fell on the 26th, immediately and, of course, normally we retreated. I went to Brdjani to my house, we handed in our weapons. The Muslims told us to hand in our weapons and they would not hurt us, so that is what we did. We went to the village, we surrendered our weapons, we signed and we went back home. We were home for 10 or 15 days, nobody bothered us until 15th June, when they came and said that we had to go to Podorasac to the playground to make statements; or rather that is when they took a list of us, they put us in a truck and took us to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Going back about the time you were in Bradina and you were telling us about a weapon, you had a weapon then at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which kind of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a M48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you tell the court who gave this weapon to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was given by Zivak Strahinja, this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did other people receive weapons on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody had some already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say briefly what was the reason for this distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody feared that the worst would happen and people were saying "you watch over your house if anyone attacks it" and that is what happened, unfortunately. It happened to me, just like that, so I had a terrible tragedy. It should not have happened, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sure. Mr. Draganic, you said you surrendered your weapon. To whom did you surrender your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My neighbour, Agan Ramic and somebody called Dzibe was there, I do not know his full name. Agan Ramic was my neighbour and we worked together in the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After that you went back to Brdjani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you were saying a while ago that on June 15th, you were arrested and taken to Celebici. Can you briefly explain the circumstances of your arrest on June 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. On 14th June, my father came to my house saying that Agan had said that I should send the keys of my car for the needs of the TO, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Draganic, slow down a little when you give us your account. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My father came to my house on 14th June in the evening, and he said that I should give my car keys because Agan wanted them. In the meantime a friend of mine, a Muslim Sefik Piria, we had worked together in Libya and he said to me "Rajko, give me your case, I look after your car". So I told my father, my father left to go to the village because my house was rather isolated, then he came back and said "give me the keys", so I sent my older son to Podorasac to find Sefik, because he had already left. Then Sefik Piria came in a car and two other people in uniform, I do not know them. Then I went to the village and we gave the keys to Agan and Asko Sultan and some others whom I do not know. I gave the keys up and he said, "you are mistreating us and we are expecting the Chetniks to kill us any moment". I said, "there are no Chetniks here" and then Agan said "tomorrow you are going to Celebici" and in fact on June 15th, I was at home, I was on my way to the cafe to meet Piria Sefik in Podorasac and my older son came after me and said, "daddy, Agan said that you had to report to the playground in Podorasac to make a statement" and I went there to the sports ground. I saw that there were already quite a number of people who had got there from the village and Spago came and he said that I had to make a statement about the car, that the car was for their needs and, of course, I signed that. Then he said "you go over there to that truck", there were other people from my village there, and then as they registered us, so we climbed into the truck and when we had all got on, they drove us off to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many people were in this truck who went to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think 60, 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately at what time did you arrive at Celebici that 15th June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We arrived maybe about 11.30 or 12.00, somewhere around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean 11.30 am or pm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the truck stop inside the camp or at the entrance of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside the camp, in front of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Would you now tell the court in detail what happened to you right after your arrival in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there the truck stopped. They took off the canvass, we came out and as we came out, we were ordered to raise our hands behind our heads and to line up against the wall. They fired over our heads with bursts of fire, and we stood there for a time, and then they said we should take two steps backwards. We did, and then we were supposed to empty our pockets, whatever we had. Some people had driving licences, IDs, some had money, our shoe laces, our belts and then again the orders came that we had to line up against the wall again, so we did. Then the order was "the first seven should follow me". I was in that group, and then they took us to some manholes. They opened a manhole --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Wait just a moment please, Mr. Draganic. Before going to this other part of the camp, let us focus on this lining up against the wall. Was that the wall near the entrance, near the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a concrete wall about three metres high between the command building and in the direction of the manholes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have to line up against the wall facing the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean all 60 or 64 of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were talking about shots being fired above your heads; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were these shots fired against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the wall, higher up. There was earth or sand or whatever there was above us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So the shots reached the grass or sand over the wall. How could you realise that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what to say. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, how do you know that the shots were fired against the grass and the sand over the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the earth and the sand would fall on our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you see or in any way realise who were the people who were shooting over your heads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I could not see that, nor do I know, nor did I dare turn around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you do not have any idea how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did these people shooting say anything while doing that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were saying something, but believe me, I cannot remember exactly what they were saying. I do not know, they were saying something, but what they were saying, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say approximately how many shots were fired on this occasion over your head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, several bursts, there were bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, how long did you remain lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour, an hour, I do not know. It seemed to me to be a long time. How long it was exactly I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said somebody took your valuables and documents from you. Did you ever get your property back after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I do not know about the others, but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Right. Now you can go ahead in your account, if you can, what happened to you right after that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, they took us to the manholes and the seven of us, we entered this manhole. It was about 4.5 metres deep, maybe it was 1 metre something wide. There was a large valve and tubes at the bottom and we spent the day there until 7.00 at night. Then there was somebody called Danilo Zelenovic and Mirko Zivak, they were elderly men and they were suffering from asthma and they were crying out. Then one of the guards said, I do not know who he was, he said "I would let you go but I dare not". Then eventually they did release Danilo Zelenovic and Mirko and they were outside and we spent time there until 7.00 at night. Then we were ordered out of the manholes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Draganic. Would you please slow down when you give us your account and let us stop for a moment to this incident of this manhole. Can you describe in more detail the manhole where you were put in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said that the manhole was about 4 to 4.5 metres deep and maybe 1 metre and something wide. At the bottom of it there were large pipes and a valve with a wheel to turn it. We spent the time from 12.00 or 1.00 until 7.00 at night. There were steps also, iron steps and there was an iron lid on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How was this lid? Was that a round lid or a square lid, a metal lid or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a metal square lid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You remember that when you were interviewed by an OTP investigator you made a drawing of this manhole. May I ask this drawing be marked for identification, I think the number is 170, Exhibit 170 for the Prosecution. May I ask this exhibit be marked and shown to the witness for identification? We have copies for your Honours, Defence lawyers. Defence lawyers have this document already.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be 170 and 171 were the documents admitted just before the break, so this is 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry. Would you please put the drawing on the ELMO so it might be seen by everybody? Thank you very much. Mr. Draganic, could you please look at this drawing. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the shaft or the manhole, the one I was telling you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many prisoners with you were put in this manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me and another six.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which position could you all maintain inside the manhole? Were you put one above the other or all together at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were at the bottom and one of us was sitting on the valve.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How could you all fit in this manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like that, we were forced to, we had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: First of all I would like to tender this Exhibit 172 for admission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have no objections to its admission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The sketch of the manhole is admitted as Exhibit 172.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Mr. Draganic, was the lid of the manhole closed over you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you breathe normally inside the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We managed because the lid did not fit too well, there was some opening, it did not fit tight, so we did have air.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you hear voices coming from outside during the time you remained in the manhole?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you give us some detail of the voices you heard on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard Zelenovic Slobodan and his father was in another manhole and Zeljko Zivak, they were calling for help, saying their fathers were choking, they had heart problems and they had asthma and they were crying for help, and later on they took them out of the manhole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean it was another manhole right in the nearby, close to yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were two or three other manholes. I do not know exactly, but there were several and they were in the manholes because we could hear them. When we came out, when we were ordered to come out, we all came out and we saw the others nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you were put into the manhole, did you see whether there were other manholes in the same area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I did see two and the third one was the one I was in. I do not know for certain because I did not dare look, maybe there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As far as I could observe, did all the manholes in that area have the same characteristics as yours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, I will object to that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, maybe they were larger manholes. They were probably larger because there were more people in them. They were probably larger. Whether they were used for the same purpose, I do not know. That I cannot know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Mr. Draganic, when you got out from your manhole could you recognise any of the guards being there, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I saw Mr. Delic, him only. I did not really work there and I did not know the people there. That was the first time I saw that. I did not really know until then, and the others I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You say Mr. Delic, do you know also the first name of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened to you right after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I left the manhole we were lined up one after the other with our hands above our heads and they took us to hangar number 6 and we were leaning against the hangar, and then groups of five were taken inside the hangar and we were told where to sit and then we went into the hangar. I was sitting on concrete, we did not have anything else. We were sitting on concrete --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Draganic. Who told you where to sit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic, Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you know that his name was Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, I would like you to give a look to the model you see in front of you. You can stand up if you wish to look at that better, and just tell us if you recognise this model.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If I may ask the usher to provide the witness with something to point at details. I would like you to point at some details you can specifically recognise, the entrance, the wall, whatever you have been talking about. If you are comfortable, you can turn around the model to see better the model.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the camp, the gate. This is the command, this was the infirmary, number 22, that is what they called it and this is number 6, this is where we were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, the witness is far from the microphone, the interpreter can hardly hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, could you please stand maybe at the side of the model with the microphone directed in your direction, so that everybody can hear you better. Could you tell us the position of the wall you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this wall (indicates), this wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you find in the model the position of the manhole and the manholes you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the manholes are these things here, if these are the manholes, those are the ones (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I think you can sit down. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately how many prisoners did you observe being in hangar 6 when you first arrived in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were -- I do not really know how many, perhaps over 200, 250, I really do not know for sure. I do not know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the number of prisoners in hangar 6 have any variation during your stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there for a short time, I was there for two and a half months, and during that time, there was almost always full. Later they moved some to the sports hall in Konjic and later I left, I was released to go home and I do not know how many were left at the time, and how many were there later after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please describe this hangar number 6, describe its physical characteristics, how it was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hangar number 6 was a military facility, garages of a kind. We sat in the hangar in four lines, and on the sides as well. I was in the third line from the door and I was the first one in the line, and at the entrance to hangar number 6, there was a bar along the hangar, I think it was used for water, for sewerage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness be provided with the photocopy of Prosecution exhibit number 1, page 7, which is a map? Can that be placed on the ELMO, please? If that might be also marked for identification, please. We have copies here available for this. Reason. (Handed). Thank you very much. Mr. Draganic, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the map of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did every prisoner have a given position inside hangar 6; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you indicate the door of the hangar on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the door (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Using this map, can you please show to the court where the prisoners were distributed in hangar 6; how were their positions organised inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please use the map on your right, and indicate on the map on your right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the door, the entrance and along here. That was the first row, the prisoners were sitting here, the second row was from here, the third row also here and this was the fourth row along the wall, and there was also a row here and from here to here (indicates) and between the rows there was a passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were talking about something with water. Could you indicate the position of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about here all along, there was a canal, a ditch with bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you personally maintain the same position during the whole period you spent in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My place was later changed by Delic, the first row, when the other people went to the sports hall about ten days before I was released to go home. Before that I had been in the same place throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to provide the witness with a pen or pencil in order to mark his positions, the witness's positions inside the hangar on this map, please? So, Mr. Draganic, I would like you to mark with an X your first position inside the hangar with the pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That was the position you maintained until ten days before leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is where I was when I arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your second position, can you also mark your second position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you put number 1 near the first mark and number 2 near the second mark, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, may I ask the witness to keep this map in front of him, because we might have other marks to add to this same exhibit during the testimony. How long did you stay in hangar 6 in all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 15th June until 30th August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How were the conditions of life in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were terrible, there were no conditions. We could not bathe for about a month, there was a lot of dust, it was very hot. The hangar was made of tin and there were -- you could not call those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How was the food supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very poor. At first, we used to receive 100 gramme pate for nine people and one loaf of bread per 13 people, and later we were allowed to receive food brought by our families, after about a month, so that was a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there any occasions when you remained without food for the entire day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: One occasion or more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How was the drinking water supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes we had it, sometimes we did not, but we mainly had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe the toilet facilities, if any? How could you relieve yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a hole dug behind the hangar and there were planks put over it and that is where we could relieve ourselves and we had nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you describe the sleeping facilities? How did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We slept on whatever we had, a blouse, some people later received blankets from their homes, sweaters, but we mainly slept on the concrete. We did not have beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you said that you were put in hangar 6 the same day of your arrival, June 15th. It was after getting out of the manhole, about what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 7.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what happened in the next few hours and in the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the next few hours after we were brought to the hangar, it was quiet that night, nothing happened, and the next day, on 16th June, they brought Scepo Gotovac. I think Mr. Delic asked, he was carrying a paper, he asked, "do you know such and such", it was two people and he said he did know them and he said "do you remember, you killed them here in 1942", I do not know which year and he said he did not. Then they started beating him --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me. When you say they started beating, who do you mean they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Delic and Zenga. They were beating him and there were another two, but them I did not know, I did not know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say at about what time of the day did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened on 16th June, perhaps around 1.30, 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did this beating take place inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were beating him inside and then they took him outdoors and later, he was unable -- I mean he had been beaten and then Delic said, or Zenga, I do not know exactly, he said that two people should come and carry him inside and they carried him into the hangar and then Zenga put an SDS badge on his forehead. He was there and in the evening they came back again. They took him outside and that was when he was beaten outside. Before that, Zenga came before the evening, he took off the SDS badge from his forehead and he asked us, "do you know what this is, what kind of a sign this is?" We kept quiet, we did not say anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, Mr. Draganic. In which position was Gotovac sitting inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gotovac was sitting in front of me when he came that day. He was sitting in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Right close to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right in front of me, he sat here in front of me (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were telling us about Zenga. Who is Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga, I know his last name is Landzo. I had not known him before, before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which role did he have, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what role he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said that Gotovac, after being beaten inside the hangar, was brought outside. What did you hear when he was outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard blows, we heard that he cried, shouted, moaned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted a while, ten, fifteen minutes, an eternity when a man is expecting something, it always takes a very long time. I really do not know exactly how many minutes it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember who returned Gotovac into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought in by Todor Zelenovic and Novak Zelenovic, those who were sitting next to the door in the first row. They brought him back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody call these two prisoners in order to let them bring back Mr. Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object, that is asked and answered. He said a while ago he did not know if it was Delic or Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, maybe I made a mistake. Did Gotovac return to his place close to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion when he came back, he sat here, in this part (indicates). That is where he sat, next to this wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean when he returned back, he sat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was laying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What distance from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about two or three metres from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe his conditions when he came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was beaten, he could not sit. He was lying down, he was asking for water. We did not have water to give him. There was none.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that the time when he had something in his forehead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who pinned this badge on his forehead?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that has been asked and answered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I wanted to be precise with what was that pinned to the forehead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a badge, a safety pin, I do not know how to call it. Perhaps there is a drawing, I made a sketch of it, I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, I am going to show the drawing you made, but can you, before that, describe the badge to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The badge was round, red, blue and white colour and SDS, there were two Ss and a D in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask this drawing be marked for identification and then shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Tell me, what is this supposed to demonstrate? Is it that it is the like of a thing that was placed on his forehead, or what is it really meant to demonstrate?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That the witness was close enough to describe the object who was pinned at the forehead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 173.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Draganic, could you look at this drawing? Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the SDS badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I tender this drawing, this document for admission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is 123, is it, for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: 173. You said that at a given point Zenga took this badge off. Before that did anybody, any prisoner try to take the badge off from Gotovac's forehead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody tried because nobody dared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Gotovac this time have any blood, specific bruises on his face or head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we did not see. He had a suit on him, he was beaten up, I know, but I did not see any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately at what time of the day did Mr. Landzo take the badge off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps 5.00 or 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anything else happen to Mr. Gotovac after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, in the evening, they took him outside. They took him out and that is where they beat him up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Draganic, can you say who took him outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the same two, Todor and Novak, because he was unable to go outside himself, and they beat him up and they shoved him back into the hangar and that is where he lay down --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Draganic, why did these two prisoners bring Mr. Gotovac outside? Did anybody tell them to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gotovac was called to go outside and he was unable to go outside himself and I think Zenga or Delic, I do not know which one, he said "the two closest to the door should carry him outside" and since they were in the first row next to the door, they picked him up and carried him outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just for the record, your Honour, is Exhibit 173 admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When Gotovac was called out and brought out for the second time that day, that was in the evening, do you remember approximately at what time of that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was perhaps 9.00, 8.30 in the evening, I do not know. It was dusk, it was not really nighttime. They called him up, again they carried him out. He was unable to go out himself, they beat him up over there and naturally when it was finished he shouted, but then he went silent. He was carried inside again, that is into the hangar and that is where he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will continue on Tuesday morning at 11.00 am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: (Court adjourned until 11.00 am on Tuesday, 9th September 1997)
